title: Why the Granth is sung
hook: the Gurus set their words in ragas so the music would carry the meaning into the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three close, and your line was the story holds us. Which story did you tell, and who heard it? A new year starts today, and it starts with sound. Day one thousand sixty-two.

Say a sentence out loud and it's over almost before it starts. Sing the same sentence and it can fill the room for a long while. Nothing in the words has changed. What changes is how long they stay in the room, and where they land when they get there. Year four on this path is called the ways of the Guru, and it opens with a plain question about a book. The Guru Granth Sahib is scripture. So why did the Gurus write it to be sung? Today: why the Granth is sung.
screen: `SPOKEN, IT'S GONE. SUNG, IT STAYS.` → `YEAR FOUR: THE WAYS OF THE GURU.` → `A BOOK MEANT TO BE SUNG.`

segments.voice: The word is raag, often written raga. Earlier on the path you met it as a mood: a set of notes and a shape of melody that can feel like dusk, or rain, or longing. This year the ragas get a block of their own, one at a time. But first, the why. Look at the headings. Above the hymns in the Granth's main body, before the first line, sits the name of a raga. The Gurus didn't leave the tune to chance. They wrote it onto the page, so the words would always arrive with their music. The Granth also says what singing does. In the fifth pauri of the Japji, Guru Nanak puts it in a short chain: sing, listen, and keep love in the mind. Then, he says, pain is sent away and peace comes home. Singing and listening stand side by side there. One voice sings, and the whole room receives it. Guru Arjan, in a salok in the var of Raag Ramkali, goes a step further. Blessed, he says in effect, are the beautiful ragas whose singing takes away all thirst. Thirst is the picture: something dry in a person that a sentence on a page doesn't always reach, and a melody can. So when Sikhs gather, the Guru's words are sung in kirtan. The meaning is the same as on the page. But a tune slows the words down. It lets a singer return to the line that matters. It lets a listener who can't follow every word still sense where the hymn is going. The tune doesn't replace the word. It carries it. That's today's line: music carries the word. Tomorrow, two small marks in those headings that tell singers how.
screen: `RAAG: A MOOD MADE OF NOTES.` · `THE RAGA WRITTEN ABOVE THE HYMN.` · `SING, LISTEN, KEEP LOVE IN THE MIND.` · then, large: `MUSIC CARRIES THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a raga without words. If you have a recording of an instrument playing a raga, a sitar, a sarangi, a flute, any slow opening without singing, start it now, softly. If you don't, listen to the longest single sound near you: a fan, a fridge, or your own voice humming one low note. Don't try to name the raga. Just follow the sound as it rises and settles. Notice where your attention goes when there's no sentence to hold on to. If you pray, you can let the word Waheguru ride on the sound once, silently. The bell holds the time.
Raag. A musical setting with its own notes and mood, written above the Guru's hymns so the words arrive with their music. Today's word.
Your line: music carries the word. Today, hum one line of a song you love, then stop, and notice how long it stays with you after. Day one thousand sixty-two.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras the Guru's hymns are sung as kirtan by ragis and by the congregation, and the raga named in each hymn's heading guides how trained musicians set it.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a raga, a musical setting with its own notes and mood, named in the headings of the Guru Granth Sahib.

trapdoor: what you thought: a raga is a background tune.
what it means: a musical setting named above each hymn, so the word and its music always travel together.

what a scholar hears: the Granth's own verses praise singing: the Japji pairs singing and listening (Ang 2), and Guru Arjan's salok in the Ramkali var blesses the ragas whose singing quenches thirst (Ang 958).
recall: the four sons of Guru Gobind Singh
